utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we hear the evidence of the next witness, there are three matters I'd like to deal with. The first two relate to oral rulings the Chamber is minded to give now. First, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling in relation to the testimony of Desimir Sarenac, scheduled as the sixth witness to testify in March 2013. The accused seeks to tender 230 associated exhibits through the witness and expects to use 15 minutes on direct examination with him. The witness's testimony was initially scheduled for January but was postponed due to the large number of documents that remained untranslated. On 15th of February, 2013, the Prosecution stated that the proposed associated exhibits were being reviewed but that there would be numerous objections to their admission. On the 25th of February, the Chamber and the accused were informed via e-mail that Prosecution would object to the admission of all of the 230 proposed associated exhibits. The Chamber simply cannot accept that such a large number of associated exhibits be tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter as it is not an efficient use of the Chamber's and the Prosecution's out-of-court time and resources. On several instances during the Prosecution's case, the Chamber proprio motu ordered that certain witnesses through whom the Prosecution was seeking the admission of large volumes of transcript be called viva voce. The same reasoning must be applied to associated exhibits. In the specific instance, the witness's statement is 20 pages long, and the proposed associated exhibits are listed in large blocks to illustrate the witness's brief comments. Just as an illustrative example, paragraph 30 of the witness's statement refers to 102 documents. This is unacceptable. Furthermore, allowing the accused to tender such a high number of associated exhibits would require the Chamber to grant an inordinate amount of time for cross-examination to the Prosecution in comparison to the time used by the accused on chief, which would run contrary to efficient trial management. This is also contrary to the Chamber's recent instruction that the accused should focus and tender only those exhibits which are really of significance to the case against him and to avoid tendering peripheral documents through Rule 92 ter statements. The Chamber thus orders that Witness Desimir Sarenac be led live. The Prosecution shall have the same time for its cross-examination as that used by the accused for its examination-in-chief. Next, the Chamber will issue a decision on the Prosecution's "Motion to Partially Exclude the Evidence of Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic," filed on the 13th of February, 2013, in which the Prosecution seeks to exclude a number of paragraphs from Vasiljevic's statement tendered under Rule 92 ter on the basis that they are irrelevant to the charges in the indictment. The accused filed his response on the 14th of February, 2013, and, having been granted to do so, the Prosecution filed its reply on the 19th of February, 2013. The Chamber has previously held that detailed evidence on military campaigns during the conflict in Croatia and on events related to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia in places other than BiH are not geographically linked to the indictment and are thus beyond the scope of this trial. As such, the following paragraphs are irrelevant to the charges against the accused and the Chamber orders that they be redacted: Part of paragraph 11, starting from the third sentence; paragraphs 12 to 18; the first sentence of paragraph 23; paragraphs 29 and 31; paragraphs 33 to 37, 40 to 46, 50 to 62; paragraph 65; paragraphs 72 to 83, 97 to 111, and 122 to 123. The Chamber reminds the accused once again that it will not admit detailed evidence on crimes against Bosnian Serbs which are not related to the crimes in the indictment. Accordingly, the Chamber also orders that paragraphs 137 and 170 be excluded from the statement. The remainder of the Prosecution's motion is therefore denied. The Chamber hereby instructs the accused to make these redactions and upload the redacted version of the statement onto e-court before Mr. Vasiljevic starts his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read a summary of Mr. Jovanovic's statement in English. [In English] His Excellency Vladislav Jovanovic was a diplomat. During his career, he was a member of various diplomatic bodies and the ambassador of the SFRY to Turkey. He was the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Serbia and FRY in July 1991 until September 1995. In September 1995, he was appointed ambassador of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the United Nations. His Excellency Jovanovic considers that before the fighting broke out in B and H, that a number of Western countries were working out a possible option for bringing the process to an end and turning Yugoslavia into a series of banana republics, and at meetings with foreign ambassadors before the violence, the independence of Slovenia and Croatia was openly advocated. He considers that the country was dissolving from within. Representatives of Slovenia, Bosnia, and Macedonia were established in addition to the SFRY ambassador. In December 1990, the Serbian people living in Croatia were stripped of their status of constituent people and instead given the title of ethnic minority. The Croatian authorities declared a political war against Serbian peoples. Serbs were dismissed from public services, and this instilled the fear in them and Ustashas also began returning to the SFRY republics. In 1991, the paramilitary formations of the new Croatian government launched unprovoked attack on the JNA, cutting off electricity, water, and food to the barracks. The JNA were constantly provoked, challenged, and assaulted. Negotiations were held, but they were unsuccessful. The Serbs in Croatia felt a need to protect themselves. His Excellency Vladislav Jovanovic's opinion is that The Hague Conference on Yugoslavia, which commenced on 7th of September 1991, had the aim to bring Yugoslavia to an end and that the Carrington paper spelt the end of Yugoslavia. Vladislav Jovanovic argued at the meeting that Yugoslavia must continue to exist and those who wanted to leave could. However, those that wanted to live together should stay together, but this was ignored. This conference, in his eyes, immediately allowed the break-up of Yugoslavia, despite the fact that there were no valid arguments to justify secession, and Slovenia and Croatia did this unconstitutionally. As Serbia's minister, he travelled Europe to explain the arguments put forth by the Serbian side in relation to the secession of the republics. However, he did not receive much support. In BH, an attempt was made to effectively deny the Serbs their status as a constituent people by out-voting them. Ambassador Cutileiro held talks in an attempt to reach an agreement between the sides. This plan was accepted by the Serbs but not by the Muslims. Other plans were drafted. However, they were not acceptable to the parties. His Excellency Vladislav Jovanovic considers that the London Conference was organised against the Serbs and the conference was not interested in resolving problems. Even at this late stage he felt that politicians did not know the true situation in BH and many were unwilling to co-operate. Talks restarted. However, no plans were acceptable to the Serbian leadership. The Muslim and Croatian leadership applied the same model as the HDZ in Croatia and blocked the JNA barracks. Vladislav Jovanovic was also aware that Bosnian Serbs were blamed for incidents that they had not caused. Vladislav Jovanovic met and spoke with President Karadzic on a number of occasions, and in the course of these conversations, he never heard anything about the idea of establishing ethnically pure Serbian national territories in BH. Karadzic supported the Cutileiro Plan that ethnic minorities remain in the cantons and there is no relocation. He emphasised that the policy was not one of shelling and targeting the city. The only plan Vladislav Jovanovic heard Karadzic talking about was one aimed at securing freedom and equality of the Serbs in Bosnia. Systematic killing and inhumane treatment of the Muslims and Croats was not the strategy of the Serbian leadership. His Excellency Vladislav Jovanovic was not aware of the existence of camps in Republika Srpska. He knew that the RS leadership had information about and discovered on a number of occasions that the International Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations were complicit in helping the opposite side with the smuggling of weapons and ammunition. He also was aware of the total exclusion zone that was set up around Sarajevo. When the Serbs responded to the Muslim's breach, they were bombed by NATO. However, this never happened to the Muslim side. The only way the VRS had to -- of ending the NATO air strikes was capturing members of the UNPROFOR as prisoners of war. Local enclaves were not demilitarised as requested, and attacks on Serbian military and civilians were mounted from these locations. Vladislav Jovanovic first learnt about the crimes in Srebrenica when a meeting of the UN Security Council was called and he ordered that a report from Belgrade be compiled. And that would be the short summary. Now I would like to pose few questions for Minister Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you were a participant in The Hague Conference on Yugoslavia in the autumn of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was left to the arbitration commission to discuss? How was the task of the arbitration commission defined on the 18th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to remind everybody that the idea of the peace conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague was presented to our side, more precisely to President Milosevic, by President Mitterrand as a form of providing good services which would not be binding upon the participants. The only thing was to try and find a common language as between brothers who were having an argument. If nothing -- if there was no success, everybody would go home out any consequences. However, this did not materialise. From the very beginning that international conference was not something that was providing good offices but, rather, imposing a solution, a solution that materialised very quickly. The conference started on the 7th of September and already on the 18th of October Lord Carrington, presiding over the conference, presented the so-called treaty provisions for convention on Yugoslavia. In that document, yes, that -- those were the provisions of an agreement on Yugoslavia, and that agreement in essence put a dot on the I on the existence of Yugoslavia and called upon all its federative republics to opt for independence and to come to Brussels, to the European Union, to get the confirmation of their independence. The decision on the disappearance of Yugoslavia was made even before the conference started, and the conference was the executor of that decision in a very fast and efficient way. It is a true blitzkrieg. Only a month was given to the federal republic to say what they had to say, and after that a solution was imposed and it was take-it-or-leave-it solution. All the other crisis all around the world last for 50 or 60 years and nobody tries to impose a solution on them within a month. In Yugoslavia it was done immediately because there was a need to come up with a pattern that would be offered to the future Soviet Union, which was dissolving at the time. So Yugoslavia was something that had to be concluded before the Soviet Union imploded. When we were there, we were brought before a fait accompli and we had to accept what had been defined beforehand, and if we did not do that we would be subjected to sanctions. Our position was that Yugoslavia existed as a state. It was one of the founders of the League of Nations and the United Nations, and nobody can -- could annul it for as long as at least half of its inhabitants were loyal to it. That was the case of Yugoslavia. However, the conference gave the entitlement to the other half that wanted to leave Yugoslavia, and those who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia were denied the right to stay in that state. That was double violence towards a state and towards peace because it was a way that paved the road to an all-out crisis in the former Yugoslavia which finally resulted in an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say that the witness said that Yugoslavia was a kind of a guinea pig, and it should be translated as a guinea pig, and it was a guinea pig for the Soviet Union. That's on line 16 on page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, did you present your position on the right of all the people to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Both President Milosevic and myself as members of the expert team and all the others -- all the other experts in all the other expert teams presented that in a very clear way. The right to self-determination is a constitutional right of the peoples who reside in Yugoslavia, and in that they were entitled to use that right in agreement with the peoples who remained in Yugoslavia and not in a violent and unilateral way. A constitutional procedure was already in place for such a case. It was not part of the constitution, but it had to be agreed before certain people wanted to secede from Yugoslavia and leave Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, not only did they not pay attention to such constitutional solutions, but they rather resorted to a unilateral and violent secession from the state, and they were supported very strongly by certain international factors from certain states, and some of them were very aggressive in their actions towards Yugoslavia as a state. I primarily mean Germany, the Vatican, Austria, and some other forces that did not shy from openly being against Yugoslavia, and let's not forget that in -- that CI in November 1990 -- like by accident circulated a secret report that envisaged that Yugoslavia would dissolve within 18 months in blood. Unfortunately, that happened almost on the dot. I don't know if anybody had that intention for Yugoslavia to be forced to embark on conflicts and violence. It remains to be seen. However, the fact is that those reports and interpretations appeared, that Yugoslavia could not remain existing as a state, and that's why it had to be eliminated from the political map in a very fast and efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, could I advise you to speak a bit more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 1, page 22, the witness said the CIA, and that was not recorded in the transcript. I would like to call up 1D20215.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, when it comes to the constitution and the provisions on self-determination, does it make a distinction between the population and the peoples or ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitution recognises the right to self-determination to every people. It does not recognise it for national minorities but for peoples. The six Yugoslav peoples that united and became Yugoslavia had that right pursuant to the constitution. However, that right could not be exercised in a unilateral and violent way, arbitrarily. There was a procedure envisaged by the constitution, and that could be done in agreement with the other peoples who wanted to stay and remain living in Yugoslavia. That procedure was not honoured. If it had been honoured, all those things that happened would not have happened, and I mean by that bloody conflicts, nor would have the international circles who were not interested in preserving Yugoslavia been able to openly meddle with Yugoslav business and to support the secession of others and work against the loyalty of some in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you look at that document, do you recognise it? Is this your document? Is this your document that you sent to the conference?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the fourth page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what did you mean when you said at line 5 and 4, "the international law on friendly relations and co-operation among the states" until the end of at that same sentence?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fourth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The right of self-determination is in that sentence. That's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first question that we as Serbia sent to Badinter's Arbitration Commission. This was a supported body to the international conference on Yugoslavia. We had three questions for them, and this one referred to the right of peoples to self-determination. Lord Carrington rephrased question 1 and question 3 without ever consulting us, and that's how he committed a kind of a violence on the original text that we submitted. Later on when we asked him why he did that, he explained that it was his right to redefine any proposals that were submitted to him. Obviously, he could not justify that right in any way or explain it by any other principle. In any case, the right to self-determination was what was the core of the crisis in Yugoslavia. Obviously some people didn't want to live with others in the same state and there was no doubt about that. Even the constitution envisaged that. The problem was how to exercise that, whether it do it in a way envisaged by the constitution or in a violent and unilateral way. On the other happened, the constitution insisted on the rights of the peoples and not on the rights of republics or territories, because their delineations were at the demarcation lines that had been established without any political significance, and those demarcation lines, those internal administrative lines were not enough. They didn't suffice for some peoples to leave Yugoslavia. They had to reach a preliminary agreement with those who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia. Serbs in Croatia and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were constituent peoples which was confirmed twice, one by the federal constitution and the other times by the republican constitutions of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina respectively, and as such they had equal rights as any other people with whom they lived together, and those were Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They had the right to self-determination if that was the case. The right as such was denied only to the Serbian constituent people in -- peoples in Serb -- in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no explanation for that. It was said that the republics of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina could secede from Yugoslavia within their then administrative borders. In other words, that the example of Yugoslavia was where they applied the principles from the former colonial Africa, when colonisers drew their borders arbitrarily later on when the peoples of Africa were liberated from the colonisers, those arbitrarily drawn borders became the borders of the states in Yugoslavia. There were no coloniser who drew any borders. Those borders were administratively arranged by the socialist Communist powers not because they wanted them to become international borders one day, the desire behind that was according to what President Tito said, "A marble lines marbley [as interpreted] cannot be broken and those lines were there to embellish the whole, not to be a separation between its parts." Unfortunately the constitutional provisions of the federal Yugoslavia were not observed and the right to self-determination were tied to territory, administrative boundaries. They declared internal boundaries as international boundaries, and they declared that international boundaries of the Yugoslavia that existed until then were null and void. This was violence against the peaceful existence of Yugoslavia, and it heralded the evil years that were to come. And it is primarily the premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia and then Bosnia-Herzegovina that contributed to that. Lord Carrington and Cyrus Vance themselves seriously warned against recognising these republics prematurely before all the necessary business had been done before that. This early premature recognition was accused by many international politicians, Kissinger, Dumas, Mitterrand. So even in the West people realised that what is being done with Yugoslavia was a very dangerous development that could lead to undesirable consequences. However that was not taken into account, because the interest of certain countries was to do away with Yugoslavia as soon as possible and to recognise the new states as soon as possible. Let us not forget that the German minister, Hans-Dietrich Genscher, was extraordinarily active at the sessions of the European Union and that he demanded by way of an ultimatum to have instant recognition of Slovenia and Croatia and that if that were not done, that the very existence of the European Community would be brought into question. Also, there were -- there was pressure exerted by the Vatican. Cardinal Sodano, who was secretary of state at the time, openly called upon Western ambassadors to have their countries momentarily recognise Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. We don't have to repeat everything that is contained in the statement, but I just wanted to ask you what this document represented on the 18th and was it taken into account? Did it yield certain effects, if you will?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, the commission did take this into account. He did not touch the second one, Lord Carrington, I mean, but the first and the third one were rephrased by him, and then the Badinter Commission in the first half of 1992 passed its well-known findings. There are 10 or 11 of them. And basically this was a death certificate for Yugoslavia, paving the way to all the former republics to be internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3020.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement before you? Do you have it in hard copy, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in hard copy. But I have it here on the screen. No, it's not on my screen. I didn't bring it because I thought that I didn't have the right to have any papers on me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll print it out for you. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 41 if you remember, and you'll see your statement in a minute, you said that the Bosnian Serbs had no intention of engaging in war, in taking part in war, and that they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D20242, could I please have that called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to explain to us the position that you presented then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this? Do you remember as Foreign Minister in Belgrade on the 30th of May when you presented these positions? I would particularly be interested in this part: [In English] "And it has been and remains principles and consistent. We are energetically opposed to all forms of violence and war." [Interpretation] Then the second and third paragraphs. Could you present that to us? What was the position that you presented then?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs in Bosnia had a maximum objective, and that is to remain in Yugoslavia as its inseparable part. In other words, they expressed full loyalty to their hitherto common state. However, this right of theirs was directly being challenged by the two other constituent peoples, the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who insisted on Bosnia leaving Yugoslavia, leaving the federation, with its entire territory. Of course the Serbs opposed that on the basis of the right they had as a constituent people, that is to say that without their agreement, such an important decision could not be made. Therefore, as far as this wish of Bosnia-Herzegovina was concerned, namely to leave the federation, it had to be discussed in accordance with the federal constitution. As we know, this was disregarded, because at the request of the European Community, the referendum was carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in contravention of the principle of consensus; namely, that there should be no out-voting among the three constituent peoples. Rather, they had to decide together on all important matters related to the future of their republic. So the Serb people as a constituent people enjoying the right to self-determination was in essence compelled to fight for this right of theirs in a situation that was changed, different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the question of this vote? How was it ultimately resolved in the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In essence the Dayton agreement rehabilitated the right of the Serb people to self-determination and enhanced their constitutional quality and was opposed to the right of the other two peoples to out-vote them. In this way, the Dayton agreement rectified an injustice for which a heavy price was paid in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we all paid a heavy price, all of us in Yugoslavia. Had the Cutileiro Plan been adopted by all, then none of this would have happened. All these terrible things would not have happened in this terrible war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Dayton succeeded because it rehabilitated the principle of self-determination and the quality of being a constituent people. Bosnia and Herzegovina was an independent state consisting of two entities. There was also a third entity that remained invisible, and that is Herceg-Bosna, and that is why this agreement was successful and that's why it was signed by all of those who were supposed to sign it. Again, I'm saying three and a half years had elapsed unnecessarily. Had the Cutileiro Plan been finalised and adopted, the Dayton agreement would not have been needed at all and war would have been totally unnecessary and all the things that happened during that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3021, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 47 of your statement, you say that you had information about the Bosnian Serbs being blamed for different incidents. Did you follow that at the time from the posts that you held? Did you -- did you manage to find anything out about that, and did you know how accurate that was?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These news about these explosions were horrific, and everyone had to be astounded by that, so many civilian casualties just because some shell fell from somewhere. And, of course, there was a divergence of views on that. As for the explosion in Vase Miskina Street and at Markale I and II, very soon the Bosnian Serbs were blamed for that. It was said that the shell had come from there, and on that basis the Bosnian Serb side was condemned even from Serbia itself, because sanctions had been imposed in part by Serbia, too, because of that, what had happened. Also, there were other things involved, so as far as the bakery was concerned, the explosion in front of the bakery, I found out that there was a report of UN secretariat that said that the shell had come from the Muslim side, not from the Serb side. As far as Markale is concerned, Yasushi Akashi who was the representative of the UN for Yugoslavia, he stated to a journalist that it was well known that the shell had arrived from the Muslim side. And later on Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the former Secretary-General of the UN, confirmed this, conveyed it to Mitterrand, namely that he was convinced that the explosion was due to a shell that had arrived from the Muslim side. So as far as Markale II is concerned, contrary to all other pressures, media pressures, that this was the result of a shell that had come from the Serb positions, artillery colonel -- an artillery colonel from the UN, I think his name was Demurenko, he presented a position that was quite different. However, he and his opinion were disregarded, ignored, and what remained was that it was only the Serb side that was to be blamed for that. As we know, Markale II was a pretext for NATO action and also for the imposition of additional sanctions on Serbian Montenegro. These are controversial matters. I learned of all of that. I did not have any direct information from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but this is the information I had, and I did notice that there were certain elements that indicated a strong suspicion in respect of these shells, namely whether they had come from the Serb side or from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity of hearing from our leadership, the leadership of Republika Srpska, about these incidents, what their information was?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sporadically when I would immediate them, and I did not have incessant contact with them. But in situations where they met with President Milosevic. Of course, I did ask about that, and I was assured by them that this was not done by the Serb forces, by the Serb side, rather, it was the Muslim side that did that, because in this way they wanted to draw international attention to the Serbs and to infuriate the international community against the Serbs and that would ultimately lead to NATO action. This was a position that was put in very strong terms by the leadership of Republika Srpska at the time. I heard that position bearing in mind that I also heard what the UN secretariat had done and Yasushi Akashi and other information that challenged or refuted the allegations that this had been done by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D20243, could we have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is your interview to Hungarian radio. I wanted to ask you about the fourth paragraph here where it says that it doesn't matter to you, it doesn't matter to Serbia what they would agree on, but, rather, it's important that they reach some agreement. Did Serbia present the Bosnian Serbs or anybody else a concept of their own in terms of the conference itself and the final solution?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbia, primarily President Milosevic, insisted that all the constituent peoples in Yugoslavia enjoyed the same right to self-determination. That was done at The Hague conference and elsewhere. However, when this unfortunate war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he insisted on the right of Serbs to freedom and equality of rights since the right to self-determination had already been endangered by war and had been denied as such by war and by the refusal to sign the Cutileiro Plan. So the Serb side advised the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs to defend their right to freedom and equality of rights and not to insist on the maximum right, and that is the right to remain in Yugoslavia if it was not possible to exercise that right. The very outbreak of the war showed that it was hard to exercise that right. Serbia throughout all the negotiations with the international mediators, Vance, Owen, Stoltenberg, and others, insisted on that, namely that a solution be found within Bosnia-Herzegovina that would equally ensure the freedom of all three peoples and that would prevent clashes among them and would prevent them turning into -- from turning into antagonist forces. This was not easy because maximum objectives were present on all sides, and the war added more vehemence to the talks that were being held, and it was hard to pursue solutions that were based on compromise. However, Serbia fully insisted on what it had insisted upon, and then that ultimately was shown in the plan of the Contact Group and at the Dayton agreement. It is not surprising that then President Clinton also gave public recognition to President Milosevic for the contributions he gave to the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the third paragraph here, you say: [In English] "Whatever we -- Carrington, whatever the agreement may be, we will accept it." [Interpretation] A bit below you say: "The conference must not be stopped before the three sides have concluded an agreement on the basis of the basic principles already adopted." Did you see any connection between these incidents and interruptions in the conference?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the conferences organised by international mediators?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The war itself was a huge obstacle to peaceful negotiations. Those forces that were not interested in finding a political solution at a certain point in time strove to prevent it by deteriorating the situation on the ground so that Lord Owen had to admit his impotence a couple of times, because very often when the gaps between sides narrowed and it looked like something can be resolved, the situation on the ground would suddenly deteriorate and the whole thing would come to a halt. The Bosnian Muslim side, which was militarily weaker in the beginning but got better equipped and stronger as time went on, was anxious to have a foreign military intervention and adapted everything to that goal, their activity on the ground and their activity in communication with other states. That was an obstacle in international negotiations that would have proceeded faster had it not been for such an expectation and objective of the Bosnian Muslim side in the civil war. However, Serbia was anxious for a political solution as soon as possible. If it failed in Lisbon with the Cutileiro Plan, they wanted it on some other occasion. So Serbia endorsed all these four or five plans and showed clearly in that way that it did not care for a territorial expansion of Serbia. It cared for stopping the war and achieving a solution that would be satisfactory to all the three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a solution that would not prejudice anyone. That was the final objective of Serbia which wanted to contribute to stopping the conflict as soon as possible and finding a solution based on the basis of accepting and respecting the right of all constituent peoples to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about this next paragraph where you say: "We all condemn the attack on the bread line," and then something about sanctions. Can you tell us, was Security Council able to find out the real truth, and how did it come about that sanctions were ultimately imposed although the truth was quite different?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at that time in my country, not in New York, but I know from what I heard that the UN secretariat had made a report, had produced a report, stating that that shell could not have arrived from the Serb side; that is to say, it could only come from the Muslim side. As far as I know, that report was not debated at that session of the Security Council. I don't know why. But one thing stands; namely, that certain members of the Security Council, primarily those aligned with the United States, were very anxious to tighten the screws on Serbia and Montenegro and by tightening the sanctions and increasing the isolation of the country. Anything was welcomed that could serve that aim, including that explosion outside the bakery. As we know, the media ascribed it to Bosnian Serbs immediately, and that was an irrevocable judgement that was not supposed to be doubted. All the conclusions to the contrary were simply ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3022, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, shall we take a break now if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you mentioned that in this Muslim tactic there was a lot of orientation towards NATO, and it was all calculated to elicit a NATO reaction. How did the NATO respond? To what extent was it responsive to that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the representatives of the Muslim side, primarily the Prime Minister Mr. Silajdzic and others advocated a military intervention, very clearly they said clearly they wanted it as soon as possible to shorten the war, but primarily it was also because the Muslim side wanted to achieve its maximum objective and an entity of two ethnic communities, and to that they adjusted the situation on the ground, and when it was necessary, incidents were created or when incidents happened such as the bakery and Markale I and II, they made the most of it to put pressure on the international community to get it to get involved and carry out a military intervention against Bosnian Serb forces. That was done quite openly. It was not concealed at all, and that was close to the heart of all these Muslim activists, and that was probably quite prominent in all their contacts with the international community. It's another matter what response they met with, but as we know, the intervention did occur in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How did -- how NATO responded is not relevant. Shall we move on. Was that your point, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was part of it. In addition, I thought it was an opportunity as well. I had ignored some suggestive questions earlier, but this one I noted was -- was a question that reformulated an earlier response that was directed to the information the witness received from the Bosnian Serb leadership and then posited as information that the witness had alluded to independent of that in the course of his testimony, which is obviously problematic. So for both those reasons I rose, but at this moment my emphasis would be on the need to take care in the formulation of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could respond to this now or later to say why this is relevant, but I'll do that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 47 you mention Markale I and the connection with the conferences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D20250.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you talk about the bakery, which specific incident do you mean? How was it known?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a bakery in the Vaso Miskin Crni street. That was the first incident where a lot of civilians were injured. It was sensational news to everyone, and of course everybody first accepted the interpretation from the Muslim side that it had been done by the Serbs. Later on came interpretations and statements made by international players that were rather contradictory. I've already mentioned that the UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali expressed his strong impression that the shell had not come from the Serb side, and Yasushi Akashi said something similar in his interview to a German newspaper. As we see, there were many different interpretations and statements, but the position ultimately taken by Western governments was that it had been done by the Serbian side, and on the basis of that a media and political propaganda against the Serbian side started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you meet on the 7th of February together with President Milosevic with Yasushi Akashi in Belgrade? Could you please look at this document and in particular the third paragraph from the bottom. [In English] "On Sunday ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I need to read only that paragraph, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, all of it. Remind us, please, what was the subject of this that was a day after Markale I. What was the topic of your discussion?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Yasushi Akashi was very pedantic and precise, and he tried to be impartial to all sides and take into account all the facts, that distinguished him in a way from others. I'm not saying that others did not try the same, but he was exceptional. He was very interested in everything going on in Bosnia, in all the incidents and the suffering of people, and he wanted to find a way to put An end to it, and in these efforts he met with complete co-operation on the Serb side, primarily President Milosevic, because he, too, wanted to put a stop to that unfortunate war for our own Serbian reasons within the country but also for humanitarian and other reasons. It says in this paragraph that a plan of the European Union that had been presented in Geneva previously was similar to another plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan supported by the European Union. As far as I remember, Muslim representatives, including the late Mr. Izetbegovic, if I remember well, were impatient to end this all by defeating the Serb side, which was impossible without a military intervention, so that Mr. Akashi was aware of all that, but his position did not allow him to take sides, and as I remember it, it was a discussion between two parties whose primary goal was to put a stop to the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3023, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you address the court, we're still on paragraph 47, the International Court of justice on account of these pressures? Paragraph 47, the second half of it. "[In English] The Muslim side in Bosnia pursued a policy ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up 1D20203.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? Could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav side, I mean the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is communicating with the international community and has prepared a report on the crimes committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and sent that report through the Security Council, but no reply was received. Perhaps it's not usual to reply. Maybe such reports are just received. In any case, we had no indication what happened with the report later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is 24th February. That's two weeks after Markale I. Do you remember this document? Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's on the screen. Is this your document? Did you send it to the International Court of Justice about NATO activities and decisions?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was sent in order to inform the International Court of Justice and for that institution to deal with it, because that operation contradicted the usual NATO commitments. It was a defensive military organisation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page 4, please. 015. Yes. Could you please look at paragraph 2 where it says that

utterances.speaker: DR. BOUTROS-GHALI
utterances.text: "[In English] It is evident that such an authorisation does not exist ..." Please comment. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would have to read first, if you will allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the middle part of paragraph 2 when it says that the right is contradicted. What does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would love to see the beginning of this document. I would like to somehow place it in time and a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Page 1 would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us when you want to move on to the following page.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now's the good time to see the following page. Thank you. Next, please. Let's see that. Please turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that here you interpret NATO's decisions, and then on page 3 and 4 are -- are your positions. Please.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you will allow me, this is about NATO's decision to use force in Sarajevo and its environs without a pre-consent being given by the Security Council. NATO's original military organisation that enjoys its status within the United Nations. However, when it comes to the use of force, the Security Council has to agree. That agreement had not been obtained, and that was the reason why we sent this warning and request to stop such things happening in the future. NATO was not authorised to act on its own when it comes to the use of force in third countries. There is a procedure which has to involve the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page to remind the witness what was requested by way of measures from the court, and then we will see the Court's answer. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you are ready, we will go to the following page where we will see the Court's reply to you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Court simply did not take our request into consideration. Somehow it excluded itself and thus it paved a way for NATO to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3024, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 63 of your statement, you speak about a conference, and that conference took place in London in the summer of 1992. You also speak about your meeting with Prime Minister Major and Minister Hogg. The last sentence in at that paragraph speaks about what you have just testified to. Did you inform the general public about that? Was it absolutely transparent that there was such a pressure put onto you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was not an international conference. It was a bilateral visit of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia whom I accompanied. Of course, we had talks with Prime Minister Major and Junior Minister Hogg. The topic was the crisis in Yugoslavia and everything that surrounded it, and since we presented our historical and legal arguments about the right of Yugoslavia to exist, and especially in the part that decided and opted for its continuation, we received a very brief and curt answer by Minister Hogg, that we could have any sort of arguments but they did not matter for them. What mattered for them, for Great Britain and the rest of the Western countries, was that we had to adopt their conclusions and decisions. Obviously we communicated that to the general public and Prime Minister Panic, who was not prepared for such a negative position towards us, but that was what had been the truth from the very beginning, from the moment when the European Union had started meddling with the crisis in Yugoslavia. Its positions were formed beforehand. The rest were just technicalities. This was just a reflection of what existed in the European Union, and that was a negative position to the existence of Yugoslavia as a federal state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number of document that he would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D20253.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness and Mr. Karadzic make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Jovanovic, can I remind you again that you need to put a pause between the questions and answers. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I don't believe the witness is speaking particularly fast, but because his answers go on for a period of time it obviously becomes difficult over time for the interpreters to keep up, so just another reminder to the witness. I don't think he's to blame in a conventional sense, but the circumstances are clearly making it difficult for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would kindly ask you to allow me not to repeat the contents of the statement. I would just like to mention the contents of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave an interview in 1994 in the month of December of that year, and the title of that interview was: "What is the Cost of Bosnia?" Do you remember that interview?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it was a long time ago. I gave a lot of interviews. It's very difficult to remember their sequence. Could you please allow me to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page 4 where you will find links to the paragraph in your statement. Please start reading the fourth paragraph which starts with the words "When former Prime Minister ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this tell you what you remember?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is it. Basically at the heart of all of those things was the fact that the European Union wanted to avoid the impression that it supports the secession of Yugoslavia. In order to achieve that, it had to proclaim Yugoslavia as a state which had disappeared, because in that case their support to the independence of the former Yugoslav states would not have been a support to secession but a form of assistance to the separate parts of a former state to obtain their own states. That's why it was necessary for all the state continuity of Yugoslavia to be interrupted. Our problem was to receive acceptance for those peoples who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia, not to -- only to stay in Yugoslavia also to continue living in that state as a state that had its continuity. Lord Carrington objected to that very energetically. He repeated on several occasions that those who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia could stay in Yugoslavia. You could -- they could call it Yugoslavia, but it had to be a new state, not the continuation of the former state and that was the essence of our problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, when Serbia advocated peace and you said that Serbia agreed to all the plans, did it express any territorial pretensions in respect of Bosnia? How did it support the Serbian side in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The position of Serbia from the beginning of the crisis was that it did not have any territorial pretensions towards the other republics, and that position was repeated by President Milosevic officially and privately, and that was the truth. The only thing that we advocated was an equal treatment of all constituent peoples and their equal rights to self-determination. When we did not fully succeed in that because there was a over-voting of Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they were forced to resist to such a nondemocratic and illegal solution. Then we started advocating an equal treatment of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On several occasions we emphasised that for Serbia everything that the three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed on about Bosnia-Herzegovina, whatever they agreed on we would accept it. When international representatives asked us for our assistance with that, we not only issued statements, but we also held them. Serbia was very constructive in corroboration to that. I can say that we supported all the peace plans from the very beginning. We never opposed any of that which was not the case with some other states; for example, the United States of America, which did not accept four of the five peace agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm charged here inter alia with my -- wanting to break up Bosnia and joining parts of it to Serbia and what is your information? What do you know about my positions on that? What were my positions? What were the positions of Serbia on that? Was the Republic of Serbia in favour of the break-up of Bosnia? Was I the one who expressed the wish to break up Yugoslavia and to join parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Serbia never had territorial pretensions towards any of the former Yugoslav republics and especially not towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. It left it to the peoples there to agree what they would do, whether they would live in an independent state or whether they would break up and leave. That was their own thing. It was not our thing. As far as I followed or statements, you firstly expressed your loyalty towards the joint state and your desire to stay in it and that was the maximum number goal that you as the supreme representative of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina advocated; however, the conditions changed and they deteriorated and you adapted the maximum goal and replaced it by a more realistic goal which was for the joint life to continue and for Bosnia to be an international entity but that all the peoples in that republic should have equal rights. That was your initial position and an ongoing position all the time. However, you encountered problems and that's why there were ups and downs in your rhetorics. However, you never expressed a desire for Republika Srpska that was being constituted to secede from Bosnia and to be merged with Yugoslavia. You considered yourself a loyal part of the joint state of Yugoslavia. There was no need for somebody to chose something that it already was and since conditions changed your position changed, and for the past several years the focus was on finding a solution within the framework of Bosnia as a separate independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency. Let's look at 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D20195.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first part is about President Bulatovic. Let's look at the second paragraph, and please tell us what is your position here? You presented that position. Please look at the paragraph. You're talking about June 1993.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In June 1993, there was a breakthrough in the efforts of international representatives of Owen-Stoltenberg who had tried to break up the stalemate. And then they first talked to Serbia and then with other participants in the peace process, and they presented their idea about the need to create a Bosnia as a union of states or a confederation or something of the sort. They presented an idea involving the percentages that its future constituent parts could keep to themselves. Obviously that plan was supported by Serbia, and after that it was presented in Zagreb and Sarajevo and so on and so forth. That was the beginning of considerations of a concept that ended up in the Dayton Accords. It was the first concept that started taking into account the ethnical principle rather than only the territorial principle. It was the first to -- to -- to see Bosnia as some sort of a confederation, at least in the initial stages, and those three sides that were very antagonistic could then approach, at the other end accept a realistic situation with time. This is what I tried to explain in this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last paragraph about the Greater Serbia. Can you please tell us whether you talked to me and the leadership of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and whether you sent such aspirations and whether Belgrade was in a position to accept those pressures on it.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That project of the Greater Serbia was imposed on Serbia as a propaganda instrument, because in that way Serbia was kept in a defensive position. Whether the others pretended to be the holders of the truth and justice. The fact is that Serbia never wanted to be a Greater Serbia. If it had wanted to be that, it would have achieved that after the First World War when the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenians were being created. If it had wanted to do that, it would have done it during the war when a meeting was held in Jajce and when a decision was made on the setting up of the federative republic of Yugoslavia. It stayed in its borders. It did not have any pretension towards the parts of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina or some other parts of what would be Yugoslavia. I believe that this part about Greater Serbia took up a lot of time for this court, inter alia, finally that manipulation with that term was abandoned. And when it comes to you and Bosnia-Herzegovina, you simply were not in a position to think along those lines because the realistic situation that you faced on the ground was such that you had to save your freedom and your equality, at that same time you had to honour the freedom and equality of the other peoples in that country. Any desire for joining Serbia was unrealistic. It was impossible. You never presented that as your idea save for at the very beginning when you emphasised that the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina considered Yugoslavia as their state and their loyalty. However, as things developed, as Bosnia-Herzegovina was acknowledged as an independent state, that position of yours and that your loyalty towards Yugoslavia as a common state was abandoned, and all that time you tied to find a solution within the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you were encouraged to do that by Serbia and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still I think you're speaking a bit too fast, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do my best to improve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you have just told us that Serbia supported us in all that. Did there come a time when there was a complete split between the leadership of Republika Srpska and the leadership of the Republic of Serbia and the federal state of Yugoslavia? What caused? What plan, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the Contact Group plan. Later on it turned out that it became 90 per cent of the future Dayton Accords. Serbia believed that that plan covered most of the needs of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska and that the part that was not covered should be left to future negotiations during peacetime, not during wartime. We in Serbia were aware that that plan was not equal handed towards Republika Srpska on the one hand and Herceg-Bosna on the other, because it allowed Herceg-Bosna to have special relations with Croatia and confederation with Croatia which was denied to Republika Srpska. What mattered for Serbia was for war to stop, for peace to be established, and that the rest of the issues should be negotiated in peacetime, and that they knew that negotiations might take time, but everything was better than to continue the war. The Serbs in Bosnia were afraid that they would be manipulated and deceived, and they did not trust that that plan would fully guarantee their freedom and equality. That is why they showed a certain resistance towards Milosevic, who did not want to procrastinate any longer, deemed that a moment had arrived for us to interrupt all political relations and others with Republika Srpska. I personally was against that, but I was not important. I was a minority. I thought that whatever negotiations could be continued were better than a lack of any negotiations and that negotiations could lead to a joint opinion and an agreement. The interaction of all relations with Republika Srpska was a total interruption. The blockade on the Drina was established. It was not officially recognised as a blockade but it was. In exchange for that, Serbia was rewarded by some sanctions being lifted, some minor ones, for an entire year, from approximately the summer of 1994 to the end of the war. The relations between Serbia and Republika Srpska did not exist. The only thing that existed was relations between Milosevic and members of parliament of Republika Srpska. Through them he tried to institute changes or, rather, shake up the leadership of Republika Srpska, but he failed. So we entered a period of very chilly relations. And that decision itself was a bad one from my point of view because a country that is under sanctions and isolation and that condemns these sanctions does not have the right to treat someone else the same way, because this automatically weakened own argumentation against sanctions. However, that was the decision made by the state leadership, and it was strictly observed all the way up until the end of the war -- or, rather, up until the end of the Dayton process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 13, the witness said "chilly relations," but he also said "non-existent."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's there at line 9. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But it was repeated in line 13, after "chilly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not counting on civility and mutual respect and things like that, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the policies were and what the political similarities were between President Milosevic and myself -- or, rather, our leadership in Bosnia? Because I have been charged with joint criminal enterprise here, that I joined up with President Milosevic and others.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the relations between President Milosevic and you personally was a sort of marriage out of necessity, because you were total antipodes politically and ideologically. It was clear that it could not last for a long time. You were more liberal. You were in favour of introducing a democratic regime without any reservations, whereas Milosevic did that, too, but with a bit of reservation. Although he himself hailed from the Communist Party, he was not an ideological extremist. On the contrary. He was very pragmatic. However, his immediate circle was still encumbered by ideological views, and that probably was a restriction upon him too. So in these relations that were not very cordial from the very outset, as far as I know -- well, they were justified from a working point of view, but they were not cordial. And between the two of you, there weren't any identical affiliations or identical views of international relations. So the decision of Milosevic to stop all contact with you and Republika Srpska and to introduce this blockade was a logical consequence of several years of - how do I put this? - it's not a lack of liking, but these are relations that -- that were not characterised by a particular cordiality or mutual sincerity, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the contacts between President Milosevic and our parliamentarians and attempts to change the government in Republika Srpska. Do you remember before and after that in the democratic processes -- or, rather, in the elections, who was it that President Milosevic supported as well as his inner circle? Which party in Republika Srpska? First of all, did he support me and the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he never explained that to me specifically, but I think he did support the Serb Democratic Party because it was the leading party and the most responsible one in the struggle of the Serb people in Bosnia for improving their position. He was not exactly thrilled by you, and there wasn't much warmth there. When he tried to remove you through your parliament, that was his - how do I put this? It was his obsession, because quite simply he could not get majority support in parliament against you. And he tried that very energetically. As a matter of fact, he even intimated to Lord Owen and others that things were almost done and that that would happen soon. So he did not realistically assess the balance of power within your parliament itself. As for others, I think that he had the late Dr. Koljevic in mind, that he could perhaps replace you if he managed to have you replaced in the first place, but that was not particularly voiced. It was just as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D20232 -- 1D2032. Could we have a look at that. Could it not be broadcast. 1D2032. And could it not be broadcast. 1D20232. So now we have the document. So could it please not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this paragraph, Serbia and Montenegro, and there's a reference to yourself there. Could you please tell us what this has to do with what you told us about a moment ago. Of course --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a reference here to Vice-President Simic and myself. I think that Vice-President Simic particularly highlighted that point regarding this replacement. I already said what things were like in Milosevic's head, if you will, and of course this was a point when relations between the two parties were at the lowest possible level. Practically there were no contacts whatsoever. So the rhetoric that is expressed here in this part a consequence of the fact that there was no relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted under seal? Can we show the top of the page so that the witness can see the institution is concerned, because he is presenting his assessments there, but please let us not make this public. Rule 70, Excellencies. That's why I asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3027 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. To the best of your knowledge and recollection, this breaking of relations and this pressure exerted by President Milosevic in respect of myself, did this reflect on the situation in Republika Srpska, especially my relations with the army and the Socialist Party in Republika Srpska and other forces? Did you have any knowledge about that, how that was reflected in that respect?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge about our internal situation in Serbia, and also I did not have any special relation about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the knowledge I received was either through the media or through contacts and meetings every now and then with the representatives of Republika Srpska in our country. Of course, I did find out certain things sometimes when I talked to Milosevic. The blockade was total, at least that's the explanation I received, and there was no possibility of doing away with that blockade. Now, whether something was done without my knowing about it, I cannot say. I can say that all parts of the system in Serbia were not in full agreement with that, and perhaps there were some small violations of that blockade from Serbia vis-a-vis Republika Srpska. I don't know about that. I can assume that such things may have happened. As far as I'm concerned, when I was in New York, when I spoke to the French Foreign Minister, I think it was Juppe at the time, when he asked me about the breaking off of all relations with Republika Srpska, he asked whether it was appropriate for them to continue communicating with representatives of Republika Srpska. I explained our situation to him as it was in terms of contacts and negotiations. I always spoke in favour of negotiations rather than breaking them off. So in an indirect way I encouraged the renewal of relations with the representatives of Republika Srpska which Milosevic did not look upon kindly, but that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber about your own knowledge about my position vis-a-vis Muslims as a whole - of course, with the exception of fundamentalism - about my relations, about my attempts to communicate with Zulfikarpasic, Filipovic, and others, such Muslim leaders, Fikret Abdic, these Muslims with a European orientation?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I know from your statements, and also a series of interviews that you gave during these years of the war and after that, it was obvious that did not have some kind of a backward view of the Muslims or of the Croats. When intolerance and antagonisms started boiling in the Bosnian parliament, you cautioned even then against crossing this red line; that is to say, abandoning talks all together and entering the dark tunnel of conflict. You also used metaphors and strong language in order to warn of this great danger that could stem from that. From the talks that I had with you every now and then, while they weren't very in-depth talks, but you never had any negative preconceptions regarding the Muslims. You only pointed out that because of the difficult experience you had with them from the past you wanted to have fully settled relations on the basis of everyone enjoying full free dough and equal rights. You indicated that several times, because in the past during the Ottoman empire, during the Second World War, and even towards the end of the socialist government when the appetites of the Muslim side in Bosnia-Herzegovina grew, you wanted to protect yourselves from such things by everyone being on their own and no one could exercise any kind of tyranny or domination. That is the position you presented to me and probably to others, both about Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D20191. Could we please have a look at that. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the first page we see your statement -- actually, two of your statements, and there's a letter. Do you remember these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can you zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 72, you speak about humanitarian matters. Can you tell us what my position was and what the position was of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with regard to humanitarian convoys and the supply of humanitarian aid to all sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as Serbia's position is concerned, and that can be confirmed by the international representatives Mr. Akashi and others, we invariably, consistently, and strictly advocated the unhindered movement of humanitarian convoys so that they could reach their proper destinations. We also indicated the possibility that it -- that they could be abused and that arms might be transported that way too. This position was repeated time and again to one and all, and all the representatives can confirm that. As for you in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you also stated your views in favour of this unhindered movement of humanitarian aid, but on the ground you heard about more things, and you were exposed to certain surprises, namely that sometimes these convoys were abused for other things like transporting weapons and so on. You stated that regularly to Milosevic and to the international representatives.
