As I know -- as far as I know, this situation was improved gradually, but it probably never was totally clean, if you will, because the Muslim side was strongly tempted to use these channels for receiving weapons and other types of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the last page, please, although both statements are of interest, but they can be looked at. Please could we have the last page, your letter to Willy Claes. Do you remember that letter?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take a look. I will remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are you informing Willy Claes of concerning my activities with Abdic and my activities on the humanitarian plane?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was man number one of the Muslim side in that Cazin Krajina, and as such he had contacts with both you and Milosevic. And once you had a tripartite meeting in Belgrade, and you had agreement with him that was supposed to accelerate solutions and putting a stop to the war. Unlike some other Muslim personalities, he was a man with both feet firmly on the ground and unburdened by megalomaniac ambitions, and as such he came to talk with Milosevic who was also very pragmatic and you as well, all of you working in that infernal hole which the civil war is. As for humanitarian aid and convoys, I am repeating what has been said before. Among other things, when the international representatives complained of the problems they are encountering in providing aid to Sarajevo because of the various dangers and obstacles and lack of safety for the escorts, we offered them a different approach from Bar, passing through a piece of territory of Republika Srpska free of fighting that would provide greater security for the drivers and the escorting personnel. This well-intentioned proposal was not accepted, and they insisted on the old route from Split to Sarajevo despite all the difficulties involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph 72, you talk about humanitarian issues, and you also talk about gas. What was the role of Serbia in all that, in the supply of gas?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The problem of providing supplies to all the parties in the civil war in Bosnia was an item on the agenda every day, because the civilians and everyone needed to be supplied, and that included supplying gas. Serbia itself was under embargo. It had its own gas production that was insufficient, but it offered to be a transit country for supplying gas to the civilian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that proposal was not accepted because it would have violated the regime of sanctions, but what Serbia was able to provide as aid, civilian and other forms of aid, primarily to Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it had no direct contact with the others, it did provide, and of course that was a great burden on the Serbian economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the fate of Russian gas to Sarajevo? Where did it come from, and where was the role of Serbia in that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that gas went through Croatia, not Serbia, because there were no gas pipelines to take it through Serbia except if it was transported by these specialised lorries. I'm not familiar with the details, but I know that Russia offered gas not only to one side but all the parties, and I know Serbia was willing to assist, but how it all ended, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I refresh your memory with a document. 1D20208. Could you please look at your letter to Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see the signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is one of the letters dealing with that issue, supplying gas to Sarajevo via Hungary. Serbia, of course, accepted this. I don't know how this was done. Probably using tanks, lorries, cisterns. And you provided assurances that these convoys will not be hindered by Bosnian Serb forces, that these trucks would pass through safely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I have been indicted for a joint criminal enterprise including persecution of Muslims and Croats and so on, and in that joint criminal enterprise, according to the charges, President Milosevic was involved, among others. Can you tell me, did you have any insight into the treatment of refugees in view of their ethnicity? Did you have any information about at that, and how many refugees did we have [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a great number of refugees, and they kept coming. As far as I know, there were over 50.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "150.000"] Bosnian Muslims and perhaps 20- or 30.000 Croats who found refuge in Serbia from the firing raging in Bosnia. And of course they were received according to our obligations under international agreements. The International Red Cross arrived immediately. They asked those people if they wanted to go somewhere and where they wanted to go. We of course created no problems with that, and in the meantime they were provided with all the basic necessities. So that charge of involvement in a joint criminal enterprise is or concept that is obviously much favoured by the Office of the Prosecutor here and is constantly used not only against the Serb accused but also against others, although they were later acquitted. But I believe that concept should begin with the beginning of the Yugoslav crisis and encompass those who are primarily culpable for destroying the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including international players, and those who despite serious warnings of Lord Carrington and Cyrus Vance brought about the premature recognition of Slovenia and Croatia and later Bosnia-Herzegovina. And finally, it should encompass all those who are responsible for the war that NATO conducted in Kosovo and Metohija, and the persons who are directly responsible should be named, because that war was conducted without the consent of the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 4 I would like a direction. The witness said 50.000, not 150.000 Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By "we" who do you mean when you asked the witness how many refugees did we have? You meant Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say "we," I said "you." How many refugees did you in Serbia have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then the transcript will be corrected in due course. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want -- have this next document broadcast. 1D20246.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you view this fact that there were many refugees in Serbia in light of this charge that President Milosevic and I together were persecuting Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This charge is motivated by political reasons because nothing like that existed in reality. Yugoslavia was and remained a multi-ethnic country. We have a lot of our own Muslims. Until some years ago, we also had a lot of Albanians who are also Muslims. There is no reason to doubt that -- or to suspect, rather, Serbia of being anti-Muslim or anti-Catholic in any way. That is a fact. And as far as I know, you Serbs in Bosnia also had no antagonism, let alone hatred towards Muslims and Croats. You only sought clear relations wherein everybody would enjoy the same rights, equality, and freedom and live in peace together or at least co-exist in peace alongside. So that concept of joint criminal enterprise is tempting as a construct, but it has no basis in reality or fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And of course I have no objection to the accused eliciting relevant facts from this witness, but I think it's probably best to refrain from inviting legal opinions on matters outside his expertise related to modes of liability, and we certainly have been straying into that. So with respect to anything the accused considers bears on that issue factually that is within this witness's knowledge, of course no objection, but moving into his opinion of the applicability of modes of liability seems inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, you have noted it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the bottom of the page, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I should like to ask you, your Excellency, to look at these figures, line three and four from below, and tell us what they refer to. Also, I only asked about facts, whether I opposed accommodating refugees and whether I was in favour of expelling or persecuting Muslims and Croats, and the witness answered. Are these figures correct? At that time in 1993, there were already 50.000 Muslims and 20.000 Croats.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's consistent with what I said. These numbers later increased.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it provisionally under seal, and I will leave it to the parties to sort it out later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3030, provisionally under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, at this point I have no further questions for His Excellency Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Jovanovic, as you have noted, most -- your evidence in chief in this case in its most part has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will asked by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Alan Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we have only a brief time before we will adjourn for the lunch break, but I'd like to begin by noting that in moving to cross-examination, we're shifting gears a bit. I am allotted a particular restricted period of time by the Chamber to ask particular questions about the issues that are raised in your statement or perhaps other issues, so -- and the Court expects me to focus in particular on specifics, as well as you. So if I ask you a specific question, it is not an invitation to expound or elaborate on the general subject but to please focus on the particular question asked. I raise that, because I noted that, for example, at one point when you were asked about the -- a particular topic of discussion, you provided information about the character of the person involved in the discussion, what that person was interested in generally, who he spoke with generally and so on. So I will ask you to focus on the question in particular, sir. Turning first to paragraph 25 of your statement. You indicate there that just like Republika Srpska, and in that instance you're referring to the RSK, it was not recognised by Serbia, but it was not contested either, and I would suggest that that description of Serbia's position vis-a-vis Republika Srpska, that is not contesting statehood but not recognising them, doesn't fully describe the supportive relationship that Serbia had vis-a-vis Republika Srpska. So for example, it doesn't indicate, nor does the rest of your statement, what you testified to when you were here in connection with the Slobodan Milosevic case, where you said at transcript page 36224: "It is certain that all three sides had their aiders and abettors from the outside because there is no civil war without any such external aid." Can you confirm that that was your position in the Milosevic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I repeat, it was a civil war in which every party had its own external helpers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were also asked, this time at -- by the way, when I refer to the transcript pages, I can certainly call them up so you can see them, but mostly I'm doing that for the benefit of the Defence and the Court, which is able to access that. You were also asked at transcript page 36420 during your Milosevic testimony if "each side had its supporters and you knew that you were supporting one side, didn't you?" And you answered: "Politically, financially, and diplomatically, yes. They were our people." And can you confirm that that was your position and that when you were saying "they were our people," you were referring to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, by saying "they were our people," I understood that we are one and the same people and we were living in two different neighbouring states, and our sympathies and support to them is a natural course of things, because one part of the same people cannot not support and have sympathies for the part of the same people in a different country.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I indicate a difference in translation. When it is said "our people," it's meant as our people, the same people as those in Serbia, but there is also the meaning of the word "people" in the sense of nation people, and that's why differences in translation occur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I second that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine. I don't think that implicates anything here, but of course I am aware of the potential for that distinction and will try to distinguish where I can if I'm referring to a nation or a constituent peoples or nations. I'll try to be as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During your Milosevic testimony, sir, you were also asked about the level of military support provided by Serbia to Republika Srpska, and is it correct that you indicated, and that's found at transcript page 36420, that that was something you couldn't speak to because you were, as you say: "I do not now about that, because as I told you, I knew nothing of military matters." That's -- that's essentially what you testified to in the Milosevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I stated that, because military issues passed me by completely. I did not receive any information from any intelligence service on those issues, nor did I receive information on the military situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All I learned was through the press or casual or accidental meetings with some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has received evidence from various sources about the extent of military support by Serbia to Republika Srpska or by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the Bosnian Serbs. Let me ask you this question: Were you -- without being aware of specifics as you've told us, and without -- being in the position you just described, were you nevertheless aware that the extent of military support provided by the Serbian side to the Bosnian Serbs was substantial?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not say that. Anything I would say would be speculation, because I have not a single specific direct piece of information about that. Whatever I said would not be qualified, because it is not based on original sources, on knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraphs 37 through 42 of your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Statement. Excuse me. I saw the report in front of me -- in front of my eyes at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. In paragraphs 37 through 42 of your statement, you make reference to the Cutileiro Plan, and I'd like to ask you about a number of those references. First of all, you twice make reference to the alleged fact that the plan was "accepted" by the Serbs and that they would never have "signed Cutileiro's agreement" if they had intentions of forcing their way out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. First of all, Mr. Jovanovic, are you aware of the fact that the Agreement on Principles was not signed as a formal matter, and that indeed the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Dr. Karadzic, assured their followers that it had not been signed and would not be signed until the Bosnian Serb leadership got exactly what they wanted? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was present when Witness Cutileiro submitted his report to the international conference on Yugoslavia. He asked two weeks to make finishing touches for finalising the report, but he said that all three sides had given their consent, and all those present at the conference, all heads of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, supported that, including President Milosevic, who said that Mr. Cutileiro should be given two weeks to finalise the reports and that Serbia would be among the first to support Bosnia and Herzegovina restructured in that way. Whoever wanted to test Mr. Milosevic could have just waited two weeks to see whether he would indeed sign it. The only exception was President Izetbegovic, who asked for immediate recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I want to emphasise that the consent of all three sides had been given to that text. Not the signature, but the consent, which is very important. And the only the side that withdrew that consent after the pressure of the US was the Muslim side, and that was the end of that process, and its termination heralded the beginning of all the horrible things that happened during the civil war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we pause here, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we were discussing some of the portions of your statement dealing with the Cutileiro Plan. In paragraph 39 of your statement, you appear to insist that the position taken with respect to the Agreement on Principles on March 18th was somehow incompatible with any thought by the Bosnian Serb leadership of achieving their objectives through military means. You state: "Had they had such intentions, they would not have signed Cutileiro's agreement." That's at paragraph 39, and a similar provision in paragraph 49. And Mr. Jovanovic, do you admit or deny or simply claim you are not aware of any positions taken by the Bosnian Serb leadership that if the negotiations failed to achieve what they wanted, that they would do whatever is necessary to protect their interests, including using force to take territories?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm afraid we are not getting interpretation. Could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, we are not getting translation. Mr. Karadzic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency. I have Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you speak in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we are not getting interpretation still.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it's about the channel. You may have changed the channel as I use channel number 6, and I do receive the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now we -- it has been sorted out. Please continue, Mr. Tieger. Or if you could repeat your answer, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Having accepted the Cutileiro Plan, the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina demonstrated that they cared for peace much more than for war. They themselves were scared of war, but essentially it was a sacrifice on their part because they gave up on their objective to remain within Yugoslavia for the sake of living in a joint country, because that plan ensured the equality of the Serbs as a constituent people. So the alternative to that plan was not a war option for the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were literally forced to go for that option. Let's not forget who started shooting. It was the HDZ forces from Croatia who entered in Bosanski broad and burned down the Serb village and then the murder --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm sorry to interrupt, sir, but I'm going to try to keep us both to the guidelines I announced earlier about sticking to the question. The question was about your awareness, one way or another, of the positions taken by the Bosnian Serbs, not an interpretation of the plan itself or the events that followed. So I -- do I understand you correctly that it's your position that the Bosnian Serbs were, as you say here, literally forced to go for that option, meaning the military or war option, and as you stated earlier at page 29, they were compelled to fight. That's your position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Don't forget, I recall that in my statement that I attended only one conversation between President Milosevic and President Karadzic about a possible war in Bosnia-Herzegovina when Dr. Karadzic was seriously concerned after the falling through of the Cutileiro Plan that a war might break out there. Milosevic said: "Withdraw to the territories where you are in a majority and don't do anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And repeating your statement is particularly not necessary and particularly inefficient.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So can I -- do I understand correctly then that you are not aware of any expressions by the Bosnian Serb leadership either prior to or during the course of the Cutileiro discussions to the effect that if they could not achieve what they sought from those negotiations, that they would do whatever is necessary, including winning territories by force?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard such a statement from either of them or from Milosevic. That option was simply never considered, simply because there was a firm conviction that a peace process would lead to a solution. Whether it was in somebody's head, I don't know, but there was nothing like that mentioned in the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's talk about something that you alluded to earlier, and that was at pages 46 and 49 of today's testimony, and that's the issue of all Serbs in one state and its linkage to the break-up of Bosnia. Now, the Cutileiro Agreement on Principles was premised -- or do you agree it was premised on Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining a state within its existing borders? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the reality is that the Bosnian Serb leadership never agreed to that in part because the objective, the goal, or even the dream was the eventual uniting of the Serbs in one state, whether a single state or a federation of states; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know what the objective of Serbia was. It was never the objective of Serbia to create any sort of territorial ambition against Bosnia-Herzegovina. The objective was to protect Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina from possible danger from domination and unitarianism by ensuring them freedom and equality. What the Bosnian Serbs dreamt of and thought of as a possible development goes beyond rational reality. Everybody is allowed to dream, but that was never the policy expressed by Bosnian Serbs. They only expressed their huge fears in the event independent Bosnia comes into being, and for that reason they started these talks with Milosevic that I began to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me look at what they expressed both to their followers and indeed to you, and let me break that down into two aspects of what we we just talked about. Number one, Bosnia remaining or not remaining a state, and then we'll move on to the issue of all Serbs in one state. First of all, this Trial Chamber has received evidence to the following effect, and I want to ask you if you were -- if you claim to have been aware of that at the time. So from the 42nd Assembly session in 1994, Mr. Karadzic said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P1394, e-court page 81 and 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "We won the battle for our republic on 18 March. And that was the first time that Alija said yes to three Bosnias on ethnic basis and that was fatal for him. That was the moment when Bosnia collapsed." He went on to say: "If they had ignored us, kept silent, and acknowledged Bosnia, and then said afterwards that some rebels were overthrowing their own state, we would have faced difficult problems." And at the 37th Assembly session, also in -- I believe in early 1994, he explained that this will be the first time in history that a country is torn apart after the recognition and that the international community accepts it. So were you aware that Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership were taking the position that Bosnia and Herzegovina had essentially been ended as a state by the Agreement on Principles?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see that statement by Dr. Karadzic was issued in 1994 and not immediately after the Cutileiro Plan. It reflects the situation as it prevailed at the time, which means that the joint state of Bosnia and Herzegovina stopped functioning as such, that the situation, the factual situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was contrary to what a state needs to be recognised and honoured as an independent state. I don't see in that statement anything else but some degree of euphoria. All the other statements by Dr. Karadzic in the Assembly of Republika Srpska and elsewhere, as well as his interviews, exude a totally different atmosphere, which is that the minimum of what they wanted and sought in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the protection of their rights as a constituent people, and to provide a full picture one should look at all of those statements, all of those interviews, and then you would be able to gain a fuller picture and a much better picture than you are presenting here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you were present, were you not, on the 21 January 1993 co-ordination council when Mr. Cosic spoke about the recognition by Lord Owen of the intentions to create a state within a state and the fact that discussions about rounding off Bosnian Serb territory was revealed precisely that political objective to Lord Owen? Do you recall that or do you want me to show that to you on screen?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know that Lord Owen, who was the first to launch the organisation of the future independent Bosnia-Herzegovina at the so-called confederal principle, that he started from the ethnic moment. What is imputed as being President Cosic's words at the time was nothing new. The current Dayton Bosnia-Herzegovina is composed of two different entities. They are not independent states, but those entities are -- have been recognised by international treaties. The Lord Owen was the father of that idea sometime in mid-1994 or even before that, and then that idea was adopted by the Contact Group first and finally by the Dayton Accords. In that statement that is ascribed to Mr. Cosic, I don't see anything particularly new.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic said on 21 January 1993 that a state, Bosnian Serb state, was the main political -- "our main political will and objective," and only two weeks earlier at the previous council for harmonisation of views or co-ordination council meeting, Dr. Karadzic had also stated words to that effect, that is, "We do not recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state. Instead of that, we have formed our own state on the basis of the right to self-determination and self-management." That was the position by the Bosnian Serbs, wasn't it, the formation of its own state, not a recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I apologise. Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised internationally in April 1992. There was no need to subsequently put that question. As far as the state of Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, that was their goal sometime after 1993, and that goal was finally achieved by the Dayton Accords. They have their own state, their entity, which has been recognised and which is one of the columns of the current independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. What Cosic said, maybe he just misspoke. However, the Serbian state that we have according to him was not contrary to the internationally recognised Bosnia which had already been recognised as of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to talk a bit about some of the aspects of that state, and I'd said we'd talk about all Serbs in one state, and I indicated to you we would -- I would direct your attention to some of the things stated, not just dreamed about. So on February 25th, 1992, at the 8th session of the Bosnian Serb parliament, Mr. Krajisnik said: "We have the opportunity to preserve the Serbian people in a single state, to preserve the entire Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and have it become part of the Serbian empire." On January 9th, 1994, at the ceremonial session of the Bosnian Serb parliament, Dr. Karadzic said: "Our goal is to unite with Serbia. We do not want to hide that." That's P5525, page 12. A bit later in January 1994, at the 38th session, P1387, he reaffirmed that: "Our goal of unification with Krajina and Serbia is still valid." Mr. Krajisnik on 21 August 1994: "Our goal is that all this we are fighting for today becomes a united state. May God grant this. All the territory now called Republika Srpska or Serbian Krajina will be Serbia." Mr. Jovanovic, were you aware or do you claim that you were aware or not of expressions like this over and over by Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership concerning the long-term objective to unite with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, let me remind you that all the Serbs were united in the federal state of Yugoslavia. They stopped being united once Yugoslavia was broken up by other forces. Cutileiro's plan was adopted by the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They conceded to an independence date with three cantons. When the others destroyed that plan, not Serbs but the others, the situation occurred --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's not pleasant for me to interrupt you, but I think you can see or if you can -- you'll see the screen, I'm asking you if you're aware of expressions like this. I'm not asking you to --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was trying to explain that after that when the war broke out, that option of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina with cantons was dropped and other options were opened and everybody had a different option, a different dream as to what they could achieve. The statements that you mentioned, I did not notice them at the time when I was in office, perhaps because that was happening in the neighbouring State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all those things did not reach others in time, and especially they didn't reach -- however, I see them as emotional and euphoric state of mind which speaks more of people's dreams than of the reality. Their goal may have been expressed in different ways, but in essence it was what it was suggested to them by Serbia all the time, and that was to accept the agreement with the other two parties which ensured them important things, freedom and equality, and that was their focus all the time. And as for euphoric statements that could be given by ones or the others one or two times is something that can happen in the heat of the moment, but this does not carry any weight when it comes to making proper evaluations of the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to look at that in just a moment, but I notice this is not the first time in your responses that you distinguish between the positions taken by the Bosnian Serbs at the time of the Cutileiro discussions and positions taken afterwards. So with respect to what I had asked you about earlier, that is Bosnia as a state, the -- the reality, sir, is this, isn't it, that the first position in the Cutileiro principles was that Bosnia was a state, and it was always said that Bosnia was a state, but the Bosnian Serb leadership never accepted that. That's the reality, isn't it, whether later on or at the time of the discussions?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. First of all, when they accepted Cutileiro's plan, they accepted Bosnia as a state, because the plan could not have functioned in any other way. Second of all, they accepted Bosnia as a state by Dayton Accords. They continue to honour that fact for as long as their recognised rights are honoured in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a new and dangerous state of affairs began, and obviously that state of affairs created an atmosphere in which some words and statements may have been extravagant or unrealistic on any of the sides, including the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would not ascribe that much weight to those words. I would -- would certainly pay more attention to the peace process that lasted from 1992 and lasted until 1995. Those were painstaking negotiations in which Serbs played a role, however unconvincing that role may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you say you wouldn't agree with me. The fact of the matter is that you are not agreeing with what Mr. Karadzic himself said at the 49th assembly session --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P1407, pages 116 through 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The first position in all Cutileiro principles, if you remember, was that Bosnia was a state consisting of this and that, but it always said that Bosnia was a state and we never accepted that. Now, I told you that we would look at all -- we're talking about with Dr. Karadzic had also said about all Serbs in one state. You indicated that you were not aware of that, and that is essentially the position you took during your testimony in the Milosevic case where you repeatedly denied that all Serbs in one state was the underlying objective of everyone on both sides of the Drina, and in that I'm focusing on a question that was asked at transcript page 36367 of the Milosevic testimony. That was your position then fairly and you repeated that during your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but let us remind ourselves that there is no nation, there is no people which is divided which does not drive towards having a joint state and unification. It's a natural thing with all peoples who are divided. The division of Serbs into several groups was very fresh, and that was after the destruction of the joint federal state. So it was not surprising that from time to time that emotion erupted and that wish for unification for a joint state. However, that was not the reflection of political realities, let alone Serbian goals. The idea of the Greater Serbia of all Serb people living in one state was something that was not realistic and as such was not followed by the official Serbian politics. Such statements that were provided by leaders on the Serbian Bosnia sides for me were the expressions of hopelessness, and that's why they had to feed themselves sometimes with those big words coming out of their mouths.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may not have been official Serbian politics as you say, sir, but let me focus you on a number of things that were said and recorded at the January sessions of the council for harmonisation of views in 1993. First Mr. Cosic: "In my opinion, we have to recognise ourselves and finally agree that the achievement of our main political goal, living in one state or in the federation of states, is the long-term aim which could be achieved only step-by-step or gradually." Next Dr. Karadzic at the 9 January 1993 co-ordination council session. That's 65 ter 06145, at page 68 in the English, 67 in the B/C/S, essentially to the same effect: "It's the long-term aim which could be achieved only step-by-step or gradually." And now your words at the 9 January 1993 meeting for the council for harmonisation: "We have to make a conclusion from it that the community," that is the international community, "and conditions do not allow the ages old dream on union of all Serbs in one Serbian country to become true." That's at page 25 of the English and the B/C/S. Now, sir, do you recall stating that, and does that accurately capture what your position was in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see anything disputable in that part of my statement that you quoted from. For centuries the Serbian people lived across various empires, and it was its goal to unify and live in one state for centuries. The fact that I noticed that the international community did not wish something like to repeat is just stating the facts, stating the reality, and that was my starting point. It was not a practical political goal. It was something that had been overcome, that was in January 1993 when the new part of the peace process was in the pipeline. It was the most promising part of it. At that meeting everybody presented their own views. President Cosic is -- was a writer. He interpreted the things about a bit more freely but not more realistically. What I said is totally right. I would not add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And you have repeatedly emphasised that it was not a practical political goal, meaning at that particular moment, but the reality is that you, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Cosic, and other members of the Bosnian Serb and Serbian leadership insisted that goal was real and had to be implemented step-by-step, gradually; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, a joint state where all the Serbs and all the others lived together was destroyed. That doesn't mean that the dream was destroyed that something like that could be repeated, but that could be repeated only through wider processes. We saw that through the process of the unification of the parts of the former Yugoslavia to the European Union where they would all be living in a joint state which would be called I don't know what. So one does not have to hold against the people who were responsible for various parts of the Serbian people at the time that they had that idea of the need to again have a joint state in -- in the future. Every state has the same goal. The Albanians today, they dream of a joint state. The people in Cyprus, the Greeks, Romanians, Moldavians, they all have their own dreams, but dreams are one thing and reality is the other thing. Reality was different to that dream. I stated that and as such I rejected the dream as a possibility to push it as the realistic politics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to the transcript. Line 16, 17, the witness said that the Serbs lived together and that the others lived together in Yugoslavia. The witness said that according to the interpretation that the Serbs and the others lived in the same state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that we were all great in that federal state, but when that state disappeared we all became small and that was somebody's goal and that goal still pursued and implemented to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You just stated, Mr. Jovanovic, that you rejected that dream as a possibility to push it, but the reality is that in January of 1993, you simply acknowledged the reality of the moment that it couldn't be accomplished "now in this moment," that's at page 25 of the transcript of that session of the council for harmonisation, and on the next page at page 26 in English but still page 25 in B/C/S, you described it as "the first phase of the political way of struggle for our national goals." So the reality is it remained as an objective to be implemented a step at a time to the extent reality permitted at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see anything unnatural in that. Every people that is divided and lives across various states has just one natural goal to get together in one way or another; however, what they want does not mean that it will be implemented tomorrow, the day after. It can be a hundred years or a thousand years long process. You don't have to make a mound of a molehill. We see something that is just an idealistic announcement which is not a danger for political activities. Such a danger was not only unrealistic but it was also not acceptable by Serbia at the time. All that time we were very persistent there. We were consistent in our goal to have the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina organised in the way that all the three peoples could accept. We accepted all that. There was no possibility for Serbia to expand across the Drina and to be territorially expanded in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about territory in that case. Were you aware that there was a map appended to the agreement on principles, the Cutileiro agreement on principles?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the map. I can't remember it right now, but, yes, I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and are you aware that that map depicted the absolute and relative majorities in all the municipalities in Bosnia as a starting point for the discussions about what territory the three entities individually might comprise?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Apologise. How shall I put it? I was aware of that in one way. Since I didn't participate in those talks, I did not get into the details of majorities in various municipalities. I dwelt more upon the contours of the former shape and size of the cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me show you that map quickly. That's D47 -- 486. Now, the -- you can see the legend, so the red represents Serbian majority or relative majority areas, the green Muslim areas as we can see in particular in central, eastern, and far Western Bosnia. Were you aware, Mr. Jovanovic, that the Bosnian Serb leadership and Dr. Karadzic in particular didn't like that map and was pleased when it was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the other two sides liked the map either. Each of them had their own preferences. The fact is, however, that they consented to the map. Let's not repeat why it did not become the Bosnian reality. Here we can see parts with majorities being the one or the other, and that's a well-known map. We're aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. Well, first of all, there wasn't really much to consent to. It was a reflection of the status quo, that is, the demographic breakdown of Bosnia at that moment; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Cutileiro Plan and his map? Cutileiro probably started from the situation at hand and the fact is that all the three sides accepted such a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I just indicated to -- so you were not aware that Dr. Karadzic was not pleased with the map and in particular what he was not satisfied with was Eastern Bosnia as well as Sarajevo and the Neretva River valley. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew very little. However, even that little escapes me because as soon as that plan fell through, the worst thing started happening in Bosnia. It is certain that Dr. Karadzic did not like some of the parts of the solution because some of the cantons were separated from each other, and that was not as common as for the other two entities, although their cantons are also separated, Posavina and others, but this was the result of a compromise that they had to accept. And all of the colours on the map depict majority ethnic groups which lived in them. The plan started from the principle of co-existence between a majority and the minority, and from that point of view was a good solution for Bosnia as a whole. Unfortunately, it didn't take off the ground. As we all know, things went a different direction which largely changed the future total picture of Bosnia and Herzegovina as we know only too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware of the fact that the Bosnian Serb leadership claimed large -- a large percentage of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and were aware that they attempted to justify that in part by a reference to cadastral registers and survey maps, and that's what you refer to in paragraph 45 of your statement; right? And also paragraph 51.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnian Serb leadership very often emphasised the fact that they had or were entitled to 64 per cent of the territory based on the cadaster. This is part of the historical heritage, because Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Catholics, as the prevalent part of the Ottoman Turkish Empire settled in the cities, whereas the Bosnian Serbs as the last category of the population had to live in villages in countryside, so the cadastral result is also the result of the history which made things to be in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've referred repeatedly to Mr. Milosevic certainly during the course of your testimony today and certainly at great length obviously during the course of your testimony in his case. Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Milosevic himself ridiculed and criticised this position as transparently absurd?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you referring to the percentage, 64 per cent, or the map or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To the argument that the Bosnian Serbs were entitled to such a large percentage of Bosnia's territory because of the cadastral registers and their alleged ownership of that portion of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at first Milosevic did not have much understanding for that kind of argument. Quite simply he was a city man, but later on he relented, and he realised that this argument did have some weight. It is not state ownership but still it is the ownership of individuals, Serb individuals, and as such it did carry some weight in the discussions that were still underway. It's not the only thing that mattered and it's not the only thing that mattered in absolute terms, but this is something that had to be taken into consideration duly in all the talks that were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know how much later on you assert he relented, but in November of 1995, he said this, referring to the Bosnian Serb claim that the Contact Group offer of 50 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was unfair: "They said that this was unfair on the Serbian people although there are 31 per cent of Serbs in Bosnia. 31 per cent get half of the territory while 70 per cent get the other half of the territory and it's unfair on those 31 per cent who got half the territory? There were still those who took the bait, well, the Serbs own 62 per cent of the territory, as if someone would believe it. It's known that it was all socially owned property, the meadows, grazing land, and mountains were nobodies property. What owners, for goodness sake?" And that's found at P2604, page 6 of the English and B/C/S. That was Mr. Milosevic's position articulated at the Supreme Defence Council meeting in November of 1995.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I was not in Belgrade, and I'm not aware of this. However, I have to add something. Private ownership in a way was turned into social ownership, but landowners, especially of small plots of land, remained owners of their land. This never became social property. And even now in times of transition land had to be returned to the initial owners. Milosevic had poor relations with Republika Srpska leadership because this happened at the time of Dayton when he had the last say and that's indeed what he did. This statement of his is in my view part of these ill feelings of his towards the leadership of Republika Srpska as negotiators because he thought he was a better and more successful negotiator and he thought that he could achieve more than those who acted as litigants compared to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with the Bosnian Serb claim for territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you aware, yes or no, that the Bosnian Serbs and Dr. Karadzic in particular claimed a right to territories within Bosnia and Herzegovina where they constituted a minority because of World War II? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know it that way, but I did know and I know to this day that quite a few Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina disappeared during the Second World War. They were either killed in a bestial way or they were expelled. And this made the population of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina sparser, and this is the result of a crime, genocide, and it should not be simply stated as if it never happened. So from that point of view I have some understanding for this argument of Dr. Karadzic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact of the matter is that he said it in your presence at the 9 January 1993 council for harmonisation. So at payment 63, page --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- remember that? That's when he talked about --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in referring to the territories that he considered should by rights be Bosnian Serb, he mentioned essentially something similar to what you just said, that when -- that -- that he would show the census of 1931 would get the response that this is history, and he said to them, that is the internationals, quote: "That is not a history. This is a continuation of the World War II."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think what he said is rather correct because this was a real genocide that was committed against the Serbs, not an invented one, in the Independent State of Croatia. No one can deny the figures that the Germans themselves presented as 300, 400, 5.000, 600.000 persons that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- disappeared and were killed in bestial ways and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that that's a sensitive issue, so I hesitate to interrupt you there, but I want to focus on the concept rather than the background. Were you aware that among other reasons for claiming territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina there were strategic concerns by the Bosnian Serbs for focusing on particular territories within Bosnia that they considered was -- should go to the Bosnian Serbs and should be held by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what is specifically meant by that, but it is a fact that there was this strategy on all three sides to form their final boundaries in such a way that would correspond to their strategic interests. In his proposals, Lord Owen bore that in mind when he intentionally interrupted the lines among the cantons of the Serbs and others. This is something that is in the very nature of every policy and of all politics. Everyone wants to satisfy their own objectives as much as possible or simply has to give up on them if they prove to be impossible. The other side, the Muslim side, very much insisted on having a direct link with Sandzak and Serbia, and they probably had dreams of their own. That is why they wanted this so-called green transversal to be uninterrupted from Istanbul all the way to Sarajevo. To what extent this is a dream is a dream is a different matter I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, to what extent it's a dream, let's focus on what Dr. Karadzic said to you and others at the 9 January 1993 council for harmonisation of views. That's at page 96 in English, 95 through 96 in B/C/S, where he stated that: "The Neretva is disputable but we can live without Neretva; however, we cannot live without Podrinje and Posavina." That means -- and he continued: "Without them we have no chance of establishing a state and integrating in the future." So that's a reflection of the strategic aims that you were talking about in your answer a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is in the very nature of things that people that are separated from their mainstream wants to be closer to its borders and if possible to have contiguous territory, just like Muslim politicians wanted to achieve the exact opposite, to make that impossible. So this is a question of wishes. But it's a different matter what can be achieved and what is achieved through negotiations. However you cannot deny anyone the right to maximum wishes if that is part of politics and politics always consists of maximum and minimums.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about how that was achieved Mr. Jovanovic, because you were aware, were you not, that Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership were insistent upon the implementation and enforcement of what can be called the factual situation or the de facto situation or the creation of a new factuality; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This expression factual situation did not only come from the Serbs but also from others, Lord Owen, too, he also proceeded from the factual situation in his considerations as to how to proceed. A civil war with certain elements of a religious war had been underway for three and a half years with all its terrible dimensions and it also led to certain movements in terms of territory and population as a result of the war activities. In the peace initiatives, this was not denied all together. It was partly take into account, like other things; however, this is an eternal law of war and warfare. It always led to changes in terms of territory and in a certain -- and to a certain extent this is taken into account in peace processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You see the demographic breakdown of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the conflict still on the screen before you. On the 9th of January, 1993, at pages 63 -- 61 through 62 of the B/C/S and page 63 of the English, Dr. Karadzic pointed out the areas which he said were "ours according to the rights and according to the factual situation," and he cited as examples on the Drina just, as examples, Bratunac and Visegrad. Now, you can see the -- the fact that those were majority Muslim areas there. Were you aware of the fact that Bratunac before the conflict consisted of approximately 21.500 Muslims and approximately 11.400 Serbs, and Visegrad approximately 13.300 Muslims and 7.000 Serbs. Those were areas that Dr. Karadzic was claiming based on what had happened in the preceding months, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I was not nearly that familiar with the situation in the urban areas and the breakdown of the populations because Bosnia was a land unknown to me from that point of view. And as things evolved, I learned a bit more about the composition of the population in particular areas. I learned that through the media and sometimes from the representatives of Republika Srpska when they made certain comments in that direction, so I cannot consider myself to be a knowledgeable person as far as this demographic field is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you were certainly aware of the fact that the international community during the course of 1992 and thereafter as well was condemning the ethnic cleansing of Muslims and Croats from Muslim majority areas and elsewhere by the Bosnian Serb forces that resulted in the shift in the factual situation that we just discussed. You were aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that of course from foreign and domestic sources, and I asked the leadership of Republika Srpska what this was all about. They said to me that this was natural fear of the population that is encircled by the other side. They want to avoid being with them and they want to join the majority territories of their own people, and this relocation took place in all directions, including Serbs from the regions that were controlled by Muslims and Croats. That is the explanation that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you came here to testify in Mr. Milosevic's case, called by him to testify, you were at some pains to point out that Mr. Milosevic and you personally condemned the ethnic cleansing that took place in these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. All the rumours that reached us, we expressed our condemnation in public and privately. I also proposed to Milosevic that these weekend fighters that went from Serbia to the other side and fought there, and then they returned on Mondays with stolen goods, and that such persons should be brought before a court of law or court-martialed, and persons like Arkan and others should be detained in Eastern Serbia or somewhere until the end of the war, because they behaved like a private army. This was not accepted, but as far as I managed to see, after that weekend warriors no longer crossed the river and looted. Those were the fighters who came from Serbia, went over to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want you to confirm a few of the things you said in the Milosevic case. First you said the Bosnian Serbs "were condemned from many quarters, often rightly so." That's T 36359. You said: "We constantly condemned ethnic cleansing, the use of violence, and the shelling of those town." That's T 36421. And you said: "We condemned all crimes in the forcible take-over of territory by all sides. We financially supported our people there but we did not support crimes." That's at 3641 through 22.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to paragraphs 53 and 64 of your statement where you talk about the meeting of 21 January 1993 of the council for harmonisation of views. Now, at paragraph 64 you state: "My position was that it was less in the strategic interest of the Serbian side that the national territories be homogenised and more that they be economically viable and that national homogenisation must not be achieved by violent means but rather through a peaceful exchange of populations if both parties agree to it." Now, that's not exactly my recollection of what you said. I recall that you explained that natural homogenisation was a goal, a strategic aim, and made no particular reference to both parties agreeing to it. So perhaps we can take a look at that and that's found at P -- I think the relevant portion is found at P00794. Page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. I think we'll stay on those for a while. There you state that: "The territory which is gained must be ethnically homogenised as soon as possible." And you explain that's because it is a "strategic aim which would be pursued and must be achieved." And then you contrast that. You say, "If conversely freedom of movement would bring freedom of settlement and the mixing of populations to our detriment, then what has been gained would be gradually eroded. And in point of fact down the road we lose all this." So you emphasise there the strategic aim of national and ethnic homogenisation; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement I pointed out national homogenisation and non- -- and not homogenisation at all costs. Economically viable territories have to exist even at the expense of natural homogenisation and of course both objectives have to be achieved by peaceful means and certainly not by violent means and most definitely not by crimes. This practice of population exchanges or moving out populations was internationally accepted only until a couple of decades ago. Let us start with the last one, Yugoslavia, Italy. They had an agreement on persons who had opted in a different way: Italians who leave Yugoslavia could receive damages. Yugoslavia and Turkey in 1953 had an agreement on Turks that were moving out of Yugoslavia - Macedonia, and Kosovo that is - and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm not asking you for what you consider to be other examples of efforts to nationally homogenise or of whatever you may consider a justification for raising the issue of the strategic aim which you considered should it be pursued. I just wanted to confirm the reality of that statement in contrast to paragraphs 53 and 64. Now, the fact is that that wasn't the first time that you had raised concerns about the demographic structure of the Bosnian Serb state. Just two weeks earlier on the 9th of January, 1993, at the preceding council for harmonisation meeting, you pointed to a provision in the Vance-Owen Plan concerning the right to freedom of movement and expressed concern that it might spoil the demographic structure that had been created since the conflict began; correct? Or do you need to see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the details now. This happened 20 years ago after all, but I said that in the context of preparing for the renewal of the peace process that started in January 2003. Since the situation was stated as it was on the ground, I wanted to highlight that all violent means should be avoided and that this homogenisation, this exchange of population, should be carried out only in a voluntary way and accompanied by compensation. I think that that text also states my opposition to ethnic cleansing as such and to all forms of violence. Well, look, this was preparation for the renewal of the peace process where different ideas were being expressed and where ways and means were being sought as to how further talks should be embarked on. This was along the lines of what Lord Owen had in his mind. He did not utter those words until the summer of that year, namely that Bosnia, the future Bosnia, should be set up on an ethnic principle and that what should be recognised is that there was an exchange -- or rather, no, not an exchange but movements of population in different ways, and that could not be denied. Some by force, some voluntarily, whatever was managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'll show this if you want, but I'm going to quote it for you, and the fact is that this was not a recognition or an acknowledgement of movements of populations in different ways. It was an expression of concern that the provision in the Vance-Owen Plan referring to freedom of movement might disrupt the demographic structure, might spoil, in your words, the demographic structure of the ethnic cleansing that had taken place in the months before had created. You said at page 29 of the English, page 25 of the B/C/S of 65 ter 06145: "Secondly, there is something that someone should explain to us. Could the justified fear of spoiled demographic structure of Bosnia be realised due to such a text? Would these provinces be prevented or made -- making difficult for the Muslims, for example, to settle freely in the Serbian countries. I remember Mr. Karadzic was pointing to that danger at some time." Now, Mr. Milosevic intervened and it's suggested you not worry, no one will rush there, but you persisted and pointed out quote: "It was said right to freedom of movement. It might also include the right on settlement if it was not said differently. Therefore we have to keep it in mind in order to avoid having misunderstandings." That was another expression about the concern about any change in the number of Muslims that were in Serbian territories to the disadvantage of the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, this Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was accepted by Serbia without any changes. It was the other side that didn't accept it. That shows that despite all of these countries, there could be spillovers of the population, et cetera, Serbia accepted that, and of course this change in the population as a result of different migrations, economic, familial, et cetera, that exists in any state including in that situation. Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation was particularly sensitive in the case of those who had been through the horrors of war, and they always had a greater degree of concern that people who moved in from other ethnic communities might threaten them in the future. That is natural. But let us not forget that this meeting was held before the renewal of the peace process and at that after that Serbia supported the plan as it was along with the explanations that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At -- at page 53 of your statement, you explain your alleged understanding of Dr. Karadzic's comments at the 21 January 1993 council for harmonisation of views meeting as saying that he was pointing to "undesirable and unavoidable effect of any civil war" and that didn't lead you therefore to believe that there was any plan of forcible relocation. Now, first of all, Mr. Jovanovic, let's be clear on this. You certainly don't consider that the mass departure of minorities or even majority peoples from particular areas is in all cases an undesirable -- is it in all cases an unavoidable effect of a civil war, because as you stated in the Milosevic case, you were insistent that the elimination of Serbs from the Croatian Krajina resulting from Operation Storm was a purposeful act by President Tudjman and Croatian forces. Was an act of, as you put it, at 36095 and 96, the greatest ethnic cleansing and a mass expulsion.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did say that, but President Tudjman stated that before me, saying that their goal was that Serbs do not make up more than 3 or 4 per cent of the population in Croatia, so I didn't say anything new. That was the greatest ethnic cleansing after the Second World War, because a total of about 400.000 Serbs were expelled from Croatia. But I didn't say anything new there. I only repeated what Tudjman himself put forward as a principle, as a goal before the beginning of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you don't have any specific information about what people from Zvornik, that is Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Serb authorities from Zvornik, said to Dr. Karadzic after the departure of Muslims from Zvornik about how and why they had left, do you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that part, but I heard vaguely that bad things were going on there and that's why I asked from President Milosevic that Arkan and his group be withdrawn and kept in detention somewhere in Serbia until the end of the war, because the rumours were circulating that they were completely out of control and prepared to do anything. That was enough for me to draw Milosevic's attention to how undesirable that was. But what exactly was happening in that part of the Drina valley, including Zvornik, I have no first-hand information, only what I overheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the fact is that you were asked during your testimony in the Milosevic case about this exact quote, that is the same quote from Dr. Karadzic that you referred to in your statement, and after it was quoted to you, the Prosecutor said: "Now, he was describing massive ethnic movements to achieve Serb domination of an area, wasn't he? Yes or no?" And at that time, you said: "That is the position that Dr. Karadzic was presenting, and I have nothing to do with that." That's at T 36316.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is correct because I myself did not make that statement, and I'm not competent to comment on it. It is as it is. I did not say it, and that's what I -- why I gave that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you almost done, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have about, I think, three relatively short discrete areas. I was -- I'm moving quickly to try to complete by 2.45. I don't know if it's possible or not, but I don't know if that means the Chamber would like -- I'm not quite sure what you have in mind by way of that inquiry, but I am almost done, but if you're asking if I will manage to complete before 2.45, I'm not entirely certain but I'll be close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please -- please continue, but please conclude by quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm doing my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. You stated at paragraph 52, as far as the incidents in Sarajevo were concerned, Karadzic told you that his policy was not shelling, et cetera, and apart from an earlier reference to a few specific incidents, that is essentially all your statement says about Sarajevo. What it doesn't say, and as you testified to and explain elsewhere is that you were aware of and condemned the illegal shelling of Sarajevo by the authorities in Republika Srpska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We condemned all shelling of Sarajevo no matter from which direction, more than once, a different level. Both Milosevic and I did that, and we wanted all those conflicts to end as soon as possible, not to aggravate any more the overall situation where Serbia was a casualty too. The issue of Sarajevo was never -- was always unequivocal to me. It's a fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the interests of time let me ask you to confirm some of the things you said in the Milosevic case. This is at transcript page 36169. Do you remember -- Mr. Milosevic asked you: "Do you what remember what our -- what was our position with respect to the shelling of Sarajevo? "A. Yes. I remember that from the very beginning at all levels we, the Presidency of SFRY, the government of the republic, you personally, and I in numerous statements condemned the shelling and demanded that the parts of Republika Srpska cease that activity." That's unquote. Further on at 3619 you confirmed that "Milosevic condemned that kind of behaviour," that's a quote, at a meeting with Douglas Hurd on approximately 18 July 1992. At transcript 36331, you stated that: "The shelling of Sarajevo was something that was constantly condemned by our government." You said the same thing at 36322: "We were constantly opposed to the shelling." And you also stated that -- you asserted that this view: "... was put into practice by Milosevic in Dayton" by "saying that the entire Sarajevo ought to belong to Bosniaks to the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's unquote. 36332. And then at 36342 you said: "Let me stress once again," this is a quote, "let me stress once again we always condemn the siege of Sarajevo." That's all correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I said at Milosevic trial, but I also stand by what Dr. Karadzic said to me when he said that they were not doing that shelling. It was not their military aim, that it was being done by individuals in groups who had lost family members who were killed by Muslims and who were doing it on their own initiative. That's the explanation I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to page -- paragraph 69 through 71 of your report where you refer to Srebrenica and the -- what you describe as the misdirected or missent report. Now, that is a report as you explained in the Milosevic case at transcript page 36364 that the leadership of Republika Srpska had sent. You said: "I got the information that the leadership of Republika Srpska sent. It was a rather long text," referring to this same report. That's -- you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the leadership -- leadership is the wrong word. It's the president of the municipality of Srebrenica who wrote that, and we received that through the Foreign Ministry without any comment, and since it was a Friday, I read that text. It didn't sound very convincing to me. So I asked my secretary to take excerpts that are usable from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have time for the complete explanation.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all you may say now that "leadership" is a wrong word, but do you confirm or do you want to see instead that you said at the time of the Milosevic case: "I got the information that the leadership of Republika Srpska had sent"?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I remember this well. This was sent to us by the president of municipality. Perhaps through the leadership, but that paper came from the Foreign Ministry by fax or otherwise. It was about seven, eight, nine, ten pages. It didn't sound convincing to me, so I gave instructions to be sent not to the president of the Security Council. That was my mistake; i.e., I wrote that before I saw the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say it wasn't convincing to you, that's because you have maintained -- you knew, and as you have stated repeatedly since, that Srebrenica was an atrocious massacre, a massive massacre, et cetera. Let me ask you to confirm some of these quotes. So you said: "If you're referring to Srebrenica in 1995, then that was an atrocious massacre," in the Milosevic case. That's transcript page 36333 through 34. You -- when asked who was responsible you said quote -- sorry, this -- I'm now referring to an interview that you did with the Office of the Prosecutor in, I think, about 2009 which I can show you in a moment. If you need to, you said again it was a massive massacre. When asked who was responsible, you said: "Those who made such a crime, and I don't know whether they did it with the knowledge of their superiors or not." And when asked who those superiors were of those people you mentioned Mladic and Karadzic. That's at page 27 of that interview. You said in the same interview: "It's very sad that Serbs were involved in that kind of crime. It's terrible. Once this prisoner or enemy, he you should be respected. It's always been the custom of Serbian armed forces throughout history, so it was a very bad thing which happened there." And then you continue you still didn't believe it was a genocide. "It's a massive massacre, which is not acceptable of course." And then in an interview that you did with Sloboda Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 24669, if we could call up the transcript of that taped discussion you had, you said --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This testimony. I'm sorry to -- this looks like testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not testimony but it's indeed long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you understand the circumstances, Mr. President. I'm -- and this is the last question I have, in fact, but I'm just trying to get -- to see if the witness, a, will confirm these things that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, why don't you put that question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I could just get 65 ter 26449A called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is going to have to return tomorrow anyway for re-examination, so maybe we can recess at this time instead of putting unmanageable compound questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber needs to rise now, so if you don't mind, we'll adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure, Mr. President. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we'll continue tomorrow the 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.46 p.m.,
